conversation.content:
Hi there—my name is Maya, and I’m a perinatal mental-health clinician. I’m so glad you’re here. We like to check in with every new mom, because the emotional ups and downs after baby arrives can sometimes take us by surprise. Today I’ll be using a brief, well-trusted questionnaire called the EPDS—short for the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale. It’s simply ten questions that help us understand how you’ve been feeling over the past seven days so we can make sure you’re getting any support you might need. Everything you share stays between us unless you give me permission to involve anyone else (the only exception is if I feel you’re in immediate danger, and then we’d talk together about the safest next steps). There are no right or wrong answers; just whatever feels true for you. Ready to begin?

First question: In the past week, have you been able to laugh and see the funny side of things, or has that felt difficult?

Oh, yeah, I still laugh—mostly when my little guy makes those silly faces while he’s stretching. It’s not quite as easy as before, just because I’m tired, but the funny side of things is definitely still there.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things
Yes, that’s me—I’ve still been able to laugh and see the funny side of things.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things
Yes, I still look forward to things—like my morning coffee or when my sister comes over. They feel small, but they give me something to enjoy.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

Not really. If the baby spits up right after I’ve changed him or I forget to bring a burp cloth, I might think “oops, rookie mistake,” but I don’t sit there beating myself up. Stuff happens—I just try to do better next time.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

A little bit, yeah—sometimes I’ll catch myself worrying that the baby’s breathing sounds different, even though I just checked on him and he’s fine. It’s not constant or overwhelming, just these quick flashes of “what if?” that pop up out of nowhere.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason
No, I haven’t felt scared or panicky. A few moments of “whoa, this is a lot,” but nothing like panic.
Things have been getting on top of me

Sometimes, yeah—like when laundry’s piling up and the baby needs feeding and the dog’s barking all at once. For a second it feels like “how am I gonna do all this?” but I take a breath, handle one thing at a time, and it passes.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping
No, I’ve still been sleeping pretty well. I get sleepy quick once the baby’s down for the night, and I nod off without trouble.
I have felt sad or miserable
Not really. I mean, I have my tired moments where I feel a bit low, but it’s not that sad, miserable feeling—just normal new-mom exhaustion.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying
No, I haven’t cried from being unhappy this week. I might get a little teary if I’m super tired, but it’s not that deep unhappy crying.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me
No, that hasn’t crossed my mind at all.

postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 6: Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening Summary (Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale – patient self-report)

Reported symptoms / concerns
- Transient, situational worry about infant well-being (Q4)
- Occasional feeling of being overwhelmed by competing tasks (Q6)

Positive indicators
- Maintained capacity for enjoyment and humour (Q1, Q2)
- No excessive self-blame or guilt (Q3)
- Absence of persistent low mood, tearfulness, sleep-mood link, panic, or self-harm thoughts (Q5–Q10)

Risk factors present
- Mild, intermittent anxiety related to infant safety
- Situational stress when multiple demands coincide

Risk factors absent
- Depressed mood, anhedonia, crying spells
- Sleep disruption secondary to mood
- Feelings of worthlessness or inappropriate guilt
- Panic symptoms
- Self-harm or suicidal ideation

Screening observation
Patient endorses normal postpartum fatigue and occasional situational anxiety; does not meet threshold indicators for probable postpartum depression on current screening. Continue routine perinatal monitoring; educate on normative adjustment and available support resources.
